title: Dry-run: shorten and redirect
intro: About 5 minutes. Two endpoints, two very different load profiles — write the arithmetic first, because it decides the key length for you.

steps.title: Derive the key length from the numbers
steps.explain: Do this before writing any code. It turns 'how long should the key be' from a guess into arithmetic, and it is the clearest demonstration that estimation drives design rather than decorating it.
steps.saysOutLoud: 182 billion URLs over five years, so 62 to the 7 — seven characters.

steps.title: Encode a counter, don't hash the URL
steps.explain: Base-62 encoding a counter makes collisions structurally impossible — no lookup, no retry loop. Hashing is stateless but needs a collision check on the write path, which reintroduces the coordination you were avoiding.

steps.title: Remove the counter bottleneck with block allocation
steps.explain: A single global sequence is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Leasing a block of 10,000 cuts coordination by 10,000× and each service spends its block locally. Gaps appear when a service restarts with unspent IDs — harmless here, because nobody is counting the URLs.
steps.saysOutLoud: I lease blocks of ten thousand so the counter isn't on the hot path.

steps.title: The write path
steps.explain: Short and boring by design — this runs at roughly a tenth of the read rate, so a little latency here is affordable. Note the mapping is immutable once created, which is what makes the read path so easy to cache.

steps.title: The read path is where the traffic is
steps.explain: Ten times the write rate, and the entries never change — so cache entries never need invalidating. That immutability makes this one of the easiest caches anyone will ever operate, and it is worth pointing out.

steps.title: 301 versus 302 is a product decision
steps.explain: The follow-up they are waiting for. A permanent redirect lets browsers cache it and skips your servers entirely next time — cheaper, but you lose click analytics. Temporary keeps every click coming to you. Frame it as analytics versus load, not as an HTTP trivia question.
steps.saysOutLoud: 301 if I want the traffic off my servers, 302 if I need the click data.

steps.title: Cache and store are separate concerns
steps.explain: Redis in front of a store sharded by key. Because links follow a steep popularity curve, a small cache absorbs the large majority of reads — and since the shard key is the same key you look up by, every read touches exactly one shard rather than scatter-gathering.

closing: If they ask about abuse: short links hide their destination, so a shortener is a phishing tool by default. Rate limit creation and check destinations against a safe-browsing list before storing.
